cefrAlignment: C1 fits: three passages of about 560–570 words on history, sociolinguistics and psychology, with argument, concession and hedging, plus mixed tasks including Yes/No/Not Given on the writer's claims, suit a C1 mock (slightly shorter than real IELTS texts).
examFidelity: Question types, instructions and word limits follow IELTS conventions. All 29 keys were checked: each has one defensible answer, Not Given items are truly absent, and No/False items contradict the text. Timers total 45 minutes.
fixes: Corrected 'about two-thirds of a full IELTS test' to about three-quarters (29 of 40 questions).
Softened 'The passages get harder, like the real test' to 'as they usually do'.
The TOEFL tip now notes that real Read an Academic Passage texts are about 200 words with 5 questions.
The heading options for Passage 2 now use roman numerals (IELTS style).

Checked the flagged facts, which are accurate as written: Conté's graphite-clay kiln process was patented in 1795 at Carnot's request during the war with Britain; Lipman's eraser-pencil patent was granted on 30 March 1858; Te Kōhanga Reo began in 1982 and inspired Hawaiian Pūnana Leo; the 2014 study (Wilson et al., Science) used a 15-minute thinking period with self-shocks, among participants who had said they would pay to avoid a shock. Also checked: the Borrowdale 1752 theft law, the 40% endangered-languages figure and the telephone-directory boredom study (Mann and Cadman).
openConcerns: The score-to-level table (25–29 = strong C1, etc.) is a rough guide, not a calibrated conversion. A specialist should check it against trial data.

Joseph Hardtmuth developed a similar graphite-clay process in Vienna around 1790. The passage calls Conté's work 'the decisive breakthrough' without claiming he was first, which is defensible but could be noted.
learnerOutcome: Learners can sit a 45-minute mixed-format mock under realistic time pressure and use their results by question type to choose what to practise next.
